title: The Last Supper
museum: Refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie (Cenacolo Vinciano), Milan
videoFormat: Step-inside-the-painting flythrough loop (9:16, 20s): along the table to Jesus, down into the wine glass, reflection loops to the start
caption:
He painted it too slowly. We're still paying for it.

Leonardo spent about three years on The Last Supper. A young friar remembered him staring at the wall for hours, then adding a stroke or two and leaving.

Fresco would never have allowed that. So he painted on a dry wall instead, and that choice is the reason it began to flake while he was still alive.

Swipe to the last slide for the irony.

Would you have rushed it?

slides.headline: He painted it too slowly.
slides.alt: Close crop of Christ's face in the Last Supper, flaking paint, a window of blue landscape behind him.

slides.headline: The Last Supper
slides.alt: The whole mural in a gold frame: thirteen figures behind a long white table in a coffered hall, a bricked-up doorway cut into the bottom centre.

slides.headline: Hours of staring. Then one stroke.
slides.alt: Leonardo's red-chalk sketch of the apostles at table as a torn paper scrap on black, above the story of Bandello watching him work.

slides.headline: Fresco doesn't wait.
slides.alt: Cream paper slide comparing true fresco (fast, wet plaster) with Leonardo's method (slow, dry wall), ending: He chose time.

slides.headline: One sentence. Twelve reactions.
slides.alt: Four stacked crops of the apostle groups, numbered 1 to 4, each with names and a one-line description.

slides.headline: The only face in shadow.
slides.alt: Close crop of Judas in dark profile beside Peter and John, a gold ring around his fist holding a small bag, with Leonardo's red-chalk head of Judas pinned at right.

slides.headline: Every line runs to his head.
slides.alt: The upper mural with gold lines along the ceiling beams and wall hangings, all converging on a small ring at Christ's head.

slides.headline: By 1517, it was already flaking.
slides.alt: Close crop of the apostle Philip pressing his hands to his chest, the paint visibly flaked away across his face and robe.

slides.headline: Then it got worse.
slides.alt: Cream paper timeline (1652, 1796, 1943, 1978–99) beside a torn scrap of Christ's sandalled feet from an early copy and a photo of the bombed refectory in 1943.

slides.headline: What made it great is destroying it.
slides.alt: Christ at the centre of the table, hands spread, flaking paint across his robe, with the closing line about the irony.

notes: Arc: Leonardo's slowness is why he refused fresco, and the dry-wall technique is why it decayed. No film plug on the last slide; only the handle is on the slides (data-chrome="handle"), no Swipe on the cover. Bandello: late, memory-based anecdote from the preface to one of his novelle; he was the nephew of the prior Vincenzo Bandello. Copy paraphrases, no quote. 1517: Antonio de Beatis, travelling with Cardinal Luigi d'Aragona, wrote that it 'is beginning to decay' (quoted on the Cenacolo museum site); Leonardo died 1519. Nail hole: secondary sources, hedged 'likely'. Vanishing-point lines drawn by eye. 'A few minutes each': visits are timed (commonly 15 min).
